    tropical fruit trees, medicinal herbs, perennial vegetables,
    Florida native plants, wildlife habitat, biomass crops, and
    community-centered growing practices share the same landscape.
  

  
    
      Host
      Cris at Finca Morada
    
    
      Published
      July 30, 2026
    
  



In the backyard portion of our visit to Finca Morada, Cris guides us
through a dense edible landscape shaped by six years of planting,
observation, propagation, pruning, and community care. Tropical fruit
trees grow beside medicinal plants, Florida natives, perennial
vegetables, pollinator species, biomass crops, and gathering spaces,
creating a food forest that supports people, wildlife, and the wider
community.



  
    Garden
    Finca Morada
  

  
    Host
    Cris
  

  
    Location
    Miami, Florida
  

  
    Climate
    Tropical South Florida
  

  
    Garden Age
    Approximately 6 Years
  

  
    Growing Style
    Layered Agroforestry
  

  
    Primary Strategy
    Diversity and Propagation
  

  
    Primary Focus
    Food, Medicine and Community
  




Inside Finca Morada’s Miami Food Forest


Finca Morada is not designed as a conventional backyard orchard.
Instead, it functions as a layered living system where food, medicine,
habitat, culture, education, and community all overlap. Fruit trees
share space with perennial vegetables, medicinal herbs, native shrubs,
pollinator plants, biomass species, and areas created for gathering
and learning.



Many of the plants serve several purposes at once. Chaya can be eaten
while also producing large amounts of material for chop-and-drop.
Firebush feeds wildlife while helping bring butterflies and
hummingbirds into the garden. Vetiver contributes biomass and remains
productive in areas where other grasses struggle with shade.
Pineapples fill gaps in the understory, while native plants create
habitat around tropical fruit trees.



The result is a food forest that reflects a broader understanding of
abundance. Productivity is measured not only by the amount of fruit
harvested, but also by how well the landscape supports people,
wildlife, relationships, education, and the sharing of plants
throughout the community.







What You’ll Learn From This Miami Food Forest



  
    How tropical fruit trees, medicinal herbs, native plants, and
    perennial vegetables can grow together in a densely layered garden
  

  
    How vetiver, chaya, Mexican sunflower, grasses, and other support
    plants contribute biomass through chop-and-drop
  

  
    Why native plants, male papaya flowers, dead wood, and mature trees
    are intentionally retained as wildlife habitat
  

  
    How shade-tolerant crops such as wild coffee, pineapples, citrus,
    and understory greens can fill lower layers of the food forest
  

  
    How cuttings, seed saving, nursery production, and plant giveaways
    help Finca Morada share perennial crops with the wider community
  

  
    How gathering spaces, workshops, graywater, and a sliding-scale
    nursery expand the purpose of a residential food forest
  








Three Highlights From the Finca Morada Tour



  

    

      
      

    

    

      A Perennial Lemon-Flavored Tea Plant

      
        Lippia alba forms a large perennial hedge and provides
        lemon-scented leaves for tea throughout the year with very
        little maintenance.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      Vetiver as a Food Forest Support Plant

      
        Vetiver tolerates more shade than many other biomass grasses,
        allowing it to remain useful for chop-and-drop in a developing
        canopy.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      Why Keep a Male Papaya Tree?

      
        Male papaya flowers support hummingbirds and hummingbird moths,
        while dead sections of the trunk can provide habitat for
        woodpeckers and other wildlife.
      

    

  






More Than a Backyard: A Community Food Forest


Many residential food forests focus primarily on producing fruit for a
single household. Finca Morada takes a broader approach. While the
garden certainly provides food, it also functions as a place for
teaching, gathering, propagation, and community resilience. Throughout
the tour, Cris explains how the landscape has gradually evolved into a
space where neighbors can learn about edible plants, purchase
propagated seedlings on a sliding scale, attend workshops, and discover
species that are rarely found in conventional nurseries.



This philosophy changes how success is measured. Instead of asking,
"How many pounds of fruit did this tree produce?" the more important
question becomes, "How many people did this garden inspire?" Every
cutting rooted, every seedling shared, and every workshop hosted allows
the impact of the food forest to spread far beyond the property lines.



As more communities begin exploring local food production, gardens like
Finca Morada demonstrate that a residential landscape can become a
valuable educational resource while still remaining productive,
beautiful, and ecologically diverse.







Medicinal Plants Are Part of the Food Forest Too


One of the defining characteristics of Finca Morada is the large number
of medicinal species growing alongside tropical fruit trees. Rather
than separating ornamental landscaping, food crops, and herbal plants
into different spaces, they are woven together throughout the garden.
This reflects a long tradition found across tropical regions where a
home landscape supplies food, medicine, shade, and habitat all at the
same time.



Visitors encounter plants such as Lippia alba, damiana, neem, noni,
moringa, Cuban oregano, and several other herbs that have long histories
of traditional use. While many of these plants are valued in cultures
around the world, they are also appreciated simply because they are
vigorous, resilient, and well adapted to South Florida's climate.



For gardeners interested in building resilient landscapes, medicinal
plants often provide additional benefits beyond their traditional uses.
Many flower for pollinators, tolerate heat, recover quickly from heavy
pruning, and supply biomass that can be returned to the soil through
chop-and-drop management.







Building Fertility Through Biomass


Healthy food forests depend on healthy soil, and one of the easiest ways
to improve soil is by continually producing organic matter within the
garden itself. Instead of relying entirely on imported mulch, many food
forest growers intentionally plant species whose primary job is to
generate leaves and stems that can be cut and laid back onto the ground.



Throughout the tour, Cris highlights plants such as vetiver, chaya, and
other vigorous growers that produce large amounts of biomass each year.
As these plants are pruned, the material becomes mulch that protects the
soil, slows evaporation, feeds microorganisms, and gradually releases
nutrients back into the ecosystem.



This process is often called chop-and-drop. Rather than
removing plant material from the garden, the nutrients remain on site
where they continue cycling through the food forest. Over time this
helps create deeper, healthier soils while reducing the need for outside
inputs.







Designing for Wildlife, Not Just Harvests


A productive food forest doesn't only support people—it also provides
habitat for birds, insects, reptiles, and beneficial pollinators.
Throughout Finca Morada, native shrubs, flowering herbs, mature trees,
and intentionally retained dead wood create places where wildlife can
feed, nest, and shelter.



One particularly interesting example is the male papaya tree featured in
the tour. Although it never produces fruit, it continues flowering and
provides nectar for hummingbirds and hummingbird moths. Rather than
removing the tree because it isn't productive in the traditional sense,
it remains an important part of the surrounding ecosystem.



This broader perspective reflects one of the core principles of food
forest design: every species should contribute something to the system.
Some plants provide fruit, others improve soil, others attract
pollinators, and some simply create habitat that increases the overall
health and resilience of the landscape.





Perennial Vegetables Fill the Spaces Between Trees


Although tropical fruit trees often receive the most attention, much of
the daily harvest from a food forest can come from perennial vegetables.
Unlike annual crops that require frequent replanting, perennial greens
continue producing for years while helping shade the soil and occupy
otherwise unused spaces beneath the tree canopy.



Throughout Finca Morada, species such as Brazilian spinach, Surinam
spinach, chaya, nopales, and arrowroot provide reliable harvests while
requiring relatively little maintenance once established. These crops
allow gardeners to harvest fresh greens throughout much of the year
without disturbing the soil every season.



Layering perennial vegetables beneath fruit trees also increases the
overall productivity of the landscape. Rather than leaving open ground,
multiple edible species occupy different levels of the food forest,
making efficient use of sunlight, water, and available growing space.







Water Is Used Carefully Throughout the Landscape


Like many successful subtropical gardens, Finca Morada demonstrates that
water management is just as important as plant selection. During the
tour, Cris discusses using graywater and thoughtful landscape design to
support long-term plant health while reducing unnecessary waste.



In climates where periods of heavy rainfall are followed by dry weather,
capturing and reusing available water helps create a more resilient
garden. Combined with dense planting, living mulch, and continuous
organic matter from chop-and-drop management, healthy soils retain
moisture longer and reduce irrigation needs over time.



While every municipality has different regulations regarding graywater,
the broader principle remains the same: keeping water cycling through
the landscape instead of allowing it to leave the property.







Propagation Multiplies the Impact of the Garden


One of the most inspiring aspects of Finca Morada is that the garden
extends far beyond the plants growing on the property. Through
propagation, seed saving, workshops, and a small nursery, many of the
species featured throughout the tour continue spreading into other
backyards across South Florida.



Rather than viewing rare edible plants as collector's items, Cris
encourages sharing them with others. Cuttings become new trees,
seedlings find new homes, and gardeners leave with both knowledge and
plants that allow them to begin creating abundance where they live.



This philosophy highlights one of the greatest strengths of food forest
gardening: every mature garden has the potential to become a nursery for
future gardens. As plants are propagated and distributed, the impact of
a single backyard continues expanding throughout the surrounding
community.







Plant Collection Summary


Finca Morada contains an impressive diversity of edible, medicinal, and
ecologically valuable species. During this tour we documented more than
thirty plants representing tropical fruit trees, perennial vegetables,
Florida native species, medicinal herbs, biomass crops, and pollinator
plants working together as one interconnected ecosystem.

The Green Yard Takeaway




Every food forest reflects the priorities of the people who build it.
Some are designed to maximize fruit production, while others focus on
rare tropical species, ornamental beauty, or self-sufficiency. Finca
Morada demonstrates another possibility: a backyard can become a place
where food, medicine, wildlife, education, and community all thrive
together.



One of the most valuable lessons from this tour is that abundance is not
measured only by harvest baskets. A food forest also produces healthy
soil, pollinator habitat, shade, seeds, cuttings, knowledge, and
relationships. As mature plants are propagated and shared, a single
garden can influence dozens—or even hundreds—of future gardens
throughout the community.



Whether you're planting your first fruit tree or designing an entire
food forest, consider including species that serve multiple purposes.
Perennial vegetables, medicinal herbs, biomass plants, and native
species all strengthen the ecosystem while making the landscape more
productive and resilient over time.

  Inside Rebel Farms: Testing What Actually Grows in Florida

  

    Florida

    New Smyrna Beach

    Food Forest Tours

    Agroforestry

    Tropical Fruit

    Zone 9B / 10A

    Rebel Farms

  

  
    Tour Rebel Farms, an experimental food forest and growing community in
    New Smyrna Beach where Tyson and Maggie are using real-world successes,
    failures, freezes, floods, and cultivar testing to learn what can
    reliably produce in this part of Florida.
  

  

    
      Hosts
      Tyson & Maggie at Rebel Farms
    

    
      Published
      August 14, 2026
    

  





Rebel Farms is an experiment in both agriculture and community. Five houses,
five families, and ten young children live as neighbors while growing food,
sharing harvests, building soil, and testing which crops can handle the
challenging combination of heat, flooding, wind, salt exposure, and occasional
hard freezes near New Smyrna Beach, Florida.





  
    Farm
    Rebel Farms
  

  
    Hosts
    Tyson & Maggie
  

  
    Location
    New Smyrna Beach, Florida
  

  
    Climate
    Border of USDA Zones 9B & 10A
  

  
    Community
    5 Houses / 5 Families
  

  
    Growing Style
    Experimental Agroforestry
  

  
    Major Challenges
    Freeze & Flooding
  

  
    Primary Goal
    Reliable Food Production at Scale
  






An Experimental Food Forest Built Around Community


Tyson describes Rebel Farms as an experiment in agriculture and community.
The project is spread through a historically suburban neighborhood where
five families live beside one another and farm together. Each household has
its own kitchen garden based on available light and growing conditions, and
the families can trade what they produce.



That same experimental approach extends into the larger food forest systems.
One area may be used to test citrus while another is planted beneath a native
oak and palm canopy. Avocados, bananas, starfruit, sapodillas, mangoes, figs,
gingers, turmeric, passion fruit, Monstera, and other crops are grown in
different situations to see what actually succeeds.



The purpose is not simply plant collecting. Rebel Farms wants data. Tyson
explains that the lessons learned on these smaller sites can guide future
plantings at a much larger scale, reducing the chance of making expensive
mistakes after hundreds of trees have already been planted.







What You’ll Learn From Rebel Farms



  
    How five neighboring families are building an agricultural community
    inside a suburban neighborhood
  

  
    Why Rebel Farms intentionally tests many citrus and fruit cultivars
    before deciding what to plant at scale
  

  
    What survived temperatures around 23–25°F and what was lost during
    a major Florida freeze
  

  
    Why Fantastic avocado moved ahead of Lula after the farm compared
    their real-world freeze performance
  

  
    How native oak and palm canopy can provide wind protection, summer
    shade, and lower water demand
  

  
    How paths, chop-and-drop, mulch, and organic matter help the system
    cope with periodic flooding
  








Calamondin: One of Rebel Farms’ Standout Citrus Trees


One tree Tyson repeatedly praises is calamondin. At Rebel Farms it has shown
the ability to grow quickly, flower heavily, and continue producing in areas
receiving only a few hours of strong sun. Tyson uses the small acidic fruit
more like a cooking lime than a sweet citrus.



The tree has also survived conditions that matter far more to Rebel Farms
than appearance alone. Tyson says their calamondin has lived through major
flooding and the recent freeze while continuing to flower and hold fruit.
Because Rebel Farms is looking for dependable production, that combination
of resilience and usefulness makes it a particularly valuable crop.







Growing Under a Native Florida Canopy


Another section of Rebel Farms uses a different strategy entirely. Native
oaks and palms remain overhead while food-producing plants fill the
understory. Tyson describes the canopy as both a windbreak and a way to
reduce intense summer sun, which also lowers water demand in a system that
currently has no permanent irrigation.



Under the canopy are rows and pockets of avocados, bananas, starfruit,
Monstera, passion fruit, gingers, turmeric, citrus, and other tropical and
subtropical crops. Material damaged by the freeze is chopped and dropped
back onto the soil rather than hauled away.



That organic material becomes part of an accumulating layer of mulch and
future compost. Because the area can experience roughly three feet of flood
water during major events, the paths also help move water toward lower
points in the property.







What a 23–25°F Freeze Taught Rebel Farms


The tour was filmed only about a month after one of the most destructive
weather events the farm had experienced. Tyson says temperatures fell into
the 23–25°F range across different microclimates and remained severely cold
for three days in a row.



The losses were substantial. Bananas died back, many gingers and turmerics
were lost, passion fruit vines were damaged, and most mangoes did not appear
likely to survive above their grafts. Jackfruit, breadfruit, ice cream bean,
tropical cherries, acerola, and Jamaican strawberry tree were among the
other casualties. Tyson estimated that roughly half of their crop was lost.



Showing that damage is important to the Rebel Farms story. This is a working
experiment, and failure changes what gets planted next. The goal is to learn
those lessons here before repeating the same mistake across a much larger
commercial planting.







Two Highlights From the Rebel Farms Tour



  

    

      
      

    

    

      Rebel Farms Tour Highlight

      
        A closer look at one of the plants, lessons, or growing systems
        featured during Part 1 of our Rebel Farms visit.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      Rebel Farms Tour Highlight

      
        Another quick lesson from Rebel Farms and its approach to testing
        crops under real Florida conditions.
      

    

  








Bananas: Productive Until the Freeze


Before the freeze, a roughly 300-square-foot area behind the pool could hold
six to twelve banana racks at one time. Tyson describes the patch as an
almost self-renewing system: new pups emerge while mature pseudostems fruit,
and after harvest the old stalk is chopped into pieces and returned to feed
the next generation.



The cultivar used heavily at Rebel Farms is Dwarf Orinoco. Tyson likes it
because it stays relatively short, handles wind and salt exposure, grows
quickly, and produces fruit that can be eaten fresh or cooked. The freeze,
however, clarified its limits. The plants died back and the farm lost around
40 racks of bananas.



Even after that failure, Tyson still considers Dwarf Orinoco one of the
better banana options they have tested for Florida because of its speed,
size, wind tolerance, salt tolerance, and ability to recover from the
ground.







Fantastic Avocado Changes the Plan


Avocados may provide the clearest example of why Rebel Farms tests plants
before scaling. Lula had previously been a favored variety, but several Lula
trees were badly damaged by the freeze. Fantastic avocado performed very
differently.



Older Fantastic trees came through the cold in good condition, held flowers,
and were already setting young avocados. Tyson says that result convinced
them to replace less reliable trees and increase future plantings of
Fantastic. Joey and Poncho were also mentioned among the cultivars that
showed strong cold tolerance.



Taste still matters, and Tyson openly notes that Fantastic is not necessarily
their favorite avocado for eating. But the farm is evaluating the whole
package: vigor, production, water tolerance, freeze tolerance, and how
quickly a tree begins providing meaningful yields.







Figs, Citrus, and Designing Around Wildlife


Rebel Farms does not evaluate every plant only as a direct harvest crop.
Figs around the avocado area are also used as a diversion for birds. The
idea is that birds arriving for fruit encounter figs first, reducing some of
the pressure on the avocado crop behind them.



Citrus is used both for production and as part of the understory. Tyson
particularly values everbearing types because they spread production across
the year instead of producing one short seasonal crop. Persian lime, Meyer
lemon, calamondin, and Lakeland limequat are among the types discussed
during the tour.



This reflects a larger design philosophy at Rebel Farms: the most valuable
plants often do more than one job. A tree can produce fruit while also
serving as shade, wind protection, wildlife diversion, pollinator support,
or part of the nutrient cycle.







Turning Chickens and Food Scraps Into Compost


The community is also working toward greater self-sufficiency in fertility.
Food scraps, weeds, and other organic material from the different families
are brought to the chicken area. The chickens break up the material, mix it,
and add manure.



Once that material reaches the right stage, it is moved into compost bins,
turned, and allowed to finish from hot compost into cold, usable compost.
The finished material is then distributed to whichever garden area needs it
most.



For Rebel Farms, this closes another loop. Household food waste and garden
waste become fertility, fertility supports new crops, and those crops feed
the families who contribute material back into the system.

The Green Yard Takeaway




Rebel Farms shows why failure can be one of the most useful parts of growing
food. A plant tag may describe a tree as cold hardy, but a real freeze can
reveal which cultivars actually survive, recover, flower, and continue
producing in a specific place.



Tyson and Maggie are using those lessons to move beyond the idea of a food
forest as something that simply looks abundant. Their goal is production:
finding plants that can reliably feed people and then applying those lessons
across larger pieces of land.



That willingness to test, lose plants, change direction, and try again is
what makes Rebel Farms such an interesting example of abundance in progress.

forests, and the systems they are developing in New Smyrna Beach. Visit
their website or follow their work online to learn more.

Tour Cedar's mature backyard food forest in Glendale, Arizona, where
years of experimentation have transformed an ordinary suburban yard
into a productive landscape filled with tropical fruit, desert-adapted
trees, backyard orchard crops, grafting experiments, and carefully
designed microclimates that make it all possible.

  

  

    
      Host
      Cedar
    

    
      Published
      December 12, 2025
    

  






Unlike many backyard orchard tours that focus only on success stories,
Cedar walks through both the victories and failures that have shaped
this Glendale food forest over many years. Nearly every tree tells a
story—whether it's an avocado finally flowering after years of waiting,
a mango surviving Arizona summers through careful placement, or an
experimental tropical species being tested simply to see what is
possible. The result is a landscape that serves as both a productive
food forest and a living laboratory for growing fruit in the Sonoran
Desert.

Inside Cedar's Glendale Backyard Food Forest


Cedar's backyard is not designed around a single gardening formula.
Instead, it has developed through years of observation, experimentation,
pruning, transplanting, grafting, and learning how individual plants
respond to Glendale's intense desert climate.



Traditional Arizona fruit trees grow beside tropical and subtropical
species that many gardeners would not expect to find in the Sonoran
Desert. Avocados, mangoes, bananas, papayas, lychees, longans, figs,
grapes, pomegranates, citrus, mulberries, apples, and experimental
seedlings all occupy carefully chosen spaces throughout the yard.



Some plants grow beneath established shade trees, while others receive
full sun once they are mature enough to tolerate it. Mulberries,
Arizona ash, citrus, desert trees, bananas, and other established plants
help soften the summer heat for younger or more sensitive fruit trees.
The resulting garden is a collection of small microclimates rather than
one uniform growing space.



What makes this tour especially useful is Cedar's willingness to discuss
the plants that struggled as openly as the plants that succeeded. He
explains where trees were burned by the sun, damaged by frost, affected
by wind, lost to root rot, attacked by pests, or simply failed to
produce worthwhile fruit. Those experiences have shaped how the garden
continues to evolve.







What You'll Learn From This Tour




How established trees can create dappled shade and protected
microclimates for tropical fruit in the Arizona desert.



Why avocados, mangoes, papayas, lychees, longans, and other sensitive
plants often perform better when they are protected while young.



How pruning a weak central leader can encourage stronger branching and
more manageable growth.



Why seedlings and grafted trees can respond differently to heat,
location, soil conditions, and seasonal stress.



How grafting allows one established tree to support multiple fruit
varieties while reducing the need for additional planting space.



Why automated irrigation and dedicated watering zones make a large,
diverse food forest easier to maintain.



How edible groundcovers such as sweet potatoes can protect soil while
also producing leaves and roots for the kitchen.



Why successful desert gardening often depends on observing each plant
individually instead of applying the same care to every tree.









A Food Forest Built Through Experimentation


Cedar approaches the backyard as a living experiment. Some trees were
planted because their fruit is already proven in Arizona, while others
were added simply to discover whether they could survive the summer
heat, winter cold, dry wind, and alkaline growing conditions.



Seedlings play an important role in that process. Mango, avocado,
loquat, longan, peach, white sapote, and other seedlings are allowed to
grow in pots or protected corners of the yard. If they remain healthy,
they may eventually become permanent trees or provide vigorous
rootstock for grafting improved varieties.



That approach reduces the pressure for every experiment to become an
immediate success. A seedling that produces disappointing fruit may
still become useful rootstock. A slow-growing tree may remain in a pot
until a better location becomes available. A tropical species that
survives without protection may reveal genetics worth preserving.



The garden therefore continues to change as Cedar learns which plants
deserve more space, which need additional protection, and which may
eventually be replaced by more productive trees.







Creating Shade and Microclimates in the Desert


Shade is one of the most important design tools in Cedar's backyard.
Rather than covering the entire garden with permanent shade cloth, he
uses a combination of established trees, temporary protection, plant
placement, and layered growth to reduce heat stress where it matters
most.



Mulberries are especially valuable because they grow rapidly and create
summer shade for nearby mangoes, papayas, avocados, and other sensitive
plants. Established desert trees, citrus, bananas, and an Arizona ash
also contribute to the canopy, creating areas that receive morning sun,
filtered afternoon light, or protection from the most intense western
exposure.



Some trees receive temporary shade cloth during their first summers.
Others are planted beneath an existing canopy with the expectation that
they will eventually grow upward into stronger sunlight as they mature.
This allows young trees to establish roots and develop woody growth
before facing the full force of an Arizona summer.



Cedar also protects exposed branches and trunks with tree paint or
mineral-based products such as Surround WP. These measures help reduce
sunburn on tender new growth, especially when temperatures rise above
110 degrees or a tree suddenly pushes beyond the protection of the
surrounding canopy.







Growing Avocados in Glendale


One of Cedar's favorite trees is a mature Fuerte avocado that spent its
early years struggling with a weak, lanky central leader. The tree
repeatedly leaned and failed to develop the stronger structure Cedar
wanted.



After he removed the central leader, the tree responded by producing a
vigorous side branch that became the new framework of the tree. Since
then, it has developed thicker wood, larger leaves, stronger growth, and
its first meaningful flowering period.



The avocado still requires protection from extreme heat and drying
winds. Cedar uses light shade cloth during summer and protects newly
exposed branches from sunburn. He has also attempted to graft Mexican
avocado genetics onto the tree, hoping to introduce additional vigor,
pollination potential, or climate tolerance.



Several avocado seedlings and young potted trees are also growing
throughout the property. Some were planted intentionally, while others
sprouted from discarded seeds. Even if these seedlings never produce
exceptional fruit, they may become valuable rootstock for future
grafting experiments.




Key lesson: A struggling avocado may respond better to
structural pruning and improved placement than to additional fertilizer.
In Cedar's garden, removing a weak central leader allowed the tree to
redirect its energy into a much stronger framework.






Mangoes, Tropical Fruit, and Continuous Experimentation


Few plants better represent Cedar's gardening philosophy than the
mangoes scattered throughout the backyard. Rather than relying on a
single variety, he grows numerous cultivars in different locations,
compares their performance, and continually experiments with grafting
new genetics onto established trees.



Southern Blush, Nam Doc Mai, Coconut Cream, and several seedling
mangoes all serve different purposes within the landscape. Some are
grown for fruit quality, others for testing cold or heat tolerance, and
some exist primarily as future rootstock capable of supporting multiple
grafted varieties.



Several trees have already demonstrated how dramatically growth can
change after structural pruning. Weak central leaders were removed,
allowing stronger side branches to become the permanent framework of the
tree. Others have been relocated into protected microclimates where
surrounding trees reduce frost damage, wind stress, and summer sunburn.



Grafting is equally important. Cedar continually adds new scions from
other growers, allowing one healthy tree to become home to several
cultivars. Instead of planting dozens of full-sized mango trees, a
single established root system can eventually produce many different
varieties while saving valuable backyard space.







Layering Tropical Fruit Into the Landscape


Although the backyard sits in Arizona's Sonoran Desert, Cedar has
carefully layered numerous tropical and subtropical species throughout
the property. Bananas, papayas, Barbados cherries, loquats, longans,
lychees, green sapote, figs, mulberries, citrus, and mangoes occupy
different niches depending on their individual needs.



Instead of forcing every tropical tree into full desert sun, many begin
life beneath existing shade trees or alongside larger plants that buffer
heat and drying winds. As the trees mature, they gradually grow upward
into brighter conditions while retaining cooler root zones below.



Even species considered difficult for Arizona—such as green sapote,
lychee, papaya, and longan—are given opportunities to succeed through
careful placement rather than assuming they cannot be grown at all.
While not every experiment survives, each one provides information that
helps shape future plantings throughout the garden.







Fruit Trees That Serve Multiple Purposes


Many of the larger trees perform far more than a single function.
Mulberries provide summer shade while also producing fruit. Citrus trees
create structure, biomass, and filtered light for neighboring tropical
species. Grapes cool fences and trellises while producing heavy summer
harvests. Groundcovers protect soil while contributing edible leaves and
roots.



This stacking of functions is one of the defining characteristics of the
food forest. Rather than assigning one purpose to each plant, Cedar
looks for species that can contribute food, shade, habitat, biomass,
rootstock, or future grafting opportunities at the same time.



As older trees mature, their role within the landscape may also change.
Some eventually become permanent canopy trees, while others are pruned
back or removed once neighboring tropical fruit can tolerate more
exposure. The garden remains flexible instead of fixed.










Key lesson: Productive food forests are rarely built by
getting everything right the first time. They evolve through years of
experimentation, observation, and adapting to how each individual plant
responds to its environment.








Plant Collection Overview



From mature orchard trees to newly planted tropical experiments,
Cedar's backyard contains one of the most diverse collections of edible
plants featured on The Green Yard. Every season brings new grafts,
additional varieties, and fresh observations about which species thrive
under desert conditions.

Lessons From Cedar's Food Forest



Perhaps the biggest takeaway from this backyard tour is that successful
desert food forests are rarely built by following a rigid plan.
Instead, they develop through years of observation, experimentation,
and a willingness to continually adapt as plants mature.





Throughout the property, Cedar demonstrates how each tree influences
the next. Shade trees protect tropical fruit, vigorous seedlings become
future grafting stock, productive trees create biomass, and every season
provides new information that shapes future decisions. Rather than
seeing the landscape as finished, he views it as an evolving ecosystem.





For gardeners living in hot climates, this tour offers practical lessons
that extend well beyond Arizona. Creating microclimates, protecting
young trees, experimenting with different cultivars, and learning from
both successes and failures are principles that can be applied almost
anywhere.





Final takeaway:

A productive food forest isn't created overnight. It grows one
experiment at a time. Cedar's backyard shows that curiosity,
observation, and patience are often just as important as choosing the

In Part 1 of our visit to Food Forest Florida, Ryan takes us through
the area he calls his Secret Garden, a productive growing space tucked
beneath mature oak trees just north of Tampa. The tour explores tropical
fruit, homemade compost, seed-grown experiments, cold protection,
banana systems, and the ways Ryan works with the existing landscape
rather than trying to replace it.

Inside Ryan’s Secret Garden


Ryan calls this section of the property his Secret Garden because it
is tucked among mature oak trees. Instead of clearing the existing
canopy to create a conventional orchard, he uses the trees as part of
the food forest’s structure.



Dying trees and fallen logs become borders for new garden beds. The
wood creates habitat for fungi and other decomposers, while unfinished
compost and wood-chip mulch gradually break down inside the beds and
form new soil.



Beneath and around the oak canopy, Ryan grows moringa, blueberries,
passion fruit, starfruit, yerba mate, bananas, malanga, beautyberry,
pineapples, citrus seedlings, avocados, mulberries, and many other
edible plants. The result is a layered garden that makes productive use
of spaces that might otherwise remain empty beneath large trees.







What You’ll Learn From Food Forest Florida



  
    How fallen logs, unfinished compost, wood chips, fungi, and
    decomposers can be combined to create productive garden beds
  

  
    Why Ryan uses mature oak trees to create shade and protection
    from wind, freezes, and severe weather
  

  
    How seed-grown citrus and avocado trees can be evaluated for
    local adaptation before being grafted
  

  
    How tropical foliage may create living winter protection around
    cold-sensitive plants such as jackfruit
  

  
    How a three-bin compost system transforms food scraps, leaves,
    and coffee grounds into fertility for fruit trees
  

  
    Why variety selection, mature size, wind tolerance, and cold
    tolerance matter when choosing bananas for Central Florida
  








Three Highlights From the Food Forest Florida Tour



  

    

      
      

    

    

      Growing Fruit Trees as Long-Term Experiments

        adaptation, and the possibility of a valuable new fruit variety.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      Could Oak Trees Help Save Florida Citrus?

      He’s Using Philodendrons to Protect a Jackfruit Tree?

      
        Ryan tests whether large tropical foliage can surround a
        sensitive jackfruit tree and provide additional protection
        during winter freezes.
      

    

  








Growing Tropical Fruit Beneath Florida Oak Trees


One of the strongest lessons from Food Forest Florida is that an
existing tree canopy does not have to prevent food production. Ryan
uses mature live oaks to create protected growing spaces with dappled
light, leaf litter, and reduced exposure to wind and cold.



A healthy seed-grown citrus tree is planted beneath the oak canopy.
Ryan believes that growing citrus from seed gives individual plants an
opportunity to express genetics that may respond differently to citrus
greening. He also discusses research into whether tannins from fallen
oak leaves may support affected citrus trees.



Pineapples are planted directly around the base of another oak tree.
Their shallow growth habit allows them to occupy space above the oak
roots, and their low-maintenance nature makes them well suited to this
protected understory location.







Growing Fruit Trees From Seed


Ryan is willing to dedicate space to fruit trees with uncertain
outcomes. Several avocados were grown from seeds taken from
store-bought or locally grown fruit. A seedling may take years to
produce and may not create fruit identical to its parent, but Ryan sees
other forms of value in the experiment.



After temperatures reached approximately 24°F, one avocado seedling
showed no visible cold damage. Even before it produces fruit, that
survival suggests that the tree is capable of growing in Ryan’s soil
and climate.



If the eventual fruit is disappointing, the established tree can still
serve as locally adapted rootstock for a proven grafted variety. Ryan
may also graft part of the tree while allowing another branch to
continue growing naturally, preserving the possibility that the
seedling could produce a worthwhile new avocado.







Experimenting With Living Cold Protection


The garden sits in USDA Zone 9B, where tropical fruit trees can be
challenged by occasional hard freezes. A Black Gold jackfruit planted
in an exposed area suffered cold damage, leading Ryan to try a
different strategy with another tree.



He planted the jackfruit beneath established philodendrons and cut
their leaves back temporarily to provide space. The goal is to allow
the jackfruit to grow during the warmer months and then let the
philodendron foliage surround it as winter approaches.



Ryan hopes this living enclosure will create a protected pocket around
the tree and provide the equivalent of a slightly warmer microclimate.
The experiment may not completely eliminate cold damage, but even a
small improvement could help tropical trees survive Central Florida
winters more reliably.







Compost, Banana Circles, and Closed-Loop Fertility


Organic material produced on and around the property is continually
returned to the food forest. Ryan uses a three-bin compost system that
begins with household food scraps, leaves, and coffee grounds collected
through a partnership with a local coffee shop.



The material moves from the freshest bin into the next stage and
eventually becomes finished compost. Ryan describes this homemade
compost as the black gold that feeds the fruit trees throughout the
property.



A banana circle provides another way to recycle yard debris. Organic
material is placed in the center of a ring of banana plants, where it
breaks down and releases nutrients into the surrounding root zone.
This allows yard waste to become fertility without needing to be
removed from the property.







Choosing Banana Varieties for Central Florida


Bananas appear throughout the Secret Garden, but Ryan does not treat
every variety as interchangeable. Taller cultivars are placed near the
house where the structure offers additional protection from wind.



The Manzano, or apple banana, is one of Ryan’s favorites for flavor. It
produces a short, sweet banana with thin skin and a green-apple note
beneath the familiar banana flavor.



For overall performance in Florida, Ryan recommends Dwarf Namwa. The
plant remains shorter than many banana cultivars and combines wind
tolerance, drought tolerance, cold tolerance, dependable production,
and good fruit quality. Its shorter stature is especially useful on a
property exposed to strong winds from a nearby lake.

The Green Yard Takeaway




Food Forest Florida shows how abundance can emerge from observation
rather than complete control. Ryan does not remove the mature oak
trees, export every piece of yard debris, or expect every seedling to
produce perfect fruit. He looks for ways each existing element can
serve another part of the system.



Oak trees become microclimates, fallen logs become garden beds, coffee
grounds become compost, yard scraps feed bananas, and experimental
seedlings may become either new varieties or locally adapted rootstock.
The garden continues to improve because Ryan is willing to test ideas,
observe the results, and let the landscape help determine what comes
next.

Finca Morada’s front yard offers an alternative to the conventional
South Florida lawn. Cris has transformed the entrance to this
half-acre North Miami property into a diverse living landscape where
regional native plants, tropical fruit, medicinal herbs, edible
groundcovers, birds, butterflies, and people all participate in the
same system.

Inside Finca Morada's Front Yard Food Forest


Most front yards are designed around turf grass and ornamental shrubs.
Finca Morada takes a very different approach. Instead of separating
native landscaping from edible gardening, this North Miami property
blends regional native plants, tropical fruit trees, medicinal species,
pollinator habitat, and edible groundcovers into one interconnected
ecosystem.



The front yard serves as an invitation to imagine what residential
landscapes could become. Rather than hiding food production behind the
house, the edible landscape becomes the first thing visitors and
neighbors experience. Every season offers a different combination of
flowers, fruit, wildlife, and changing plant communities that continue
to mature together.



This approach also challenges the idea that gardeners must choose
between growing native plants or edible plants. At Finca Morada, both
can coexist. Native trees and shrubs create habitat for birds and
pollinators while tropical fruit trees, medicinal herbs, and perennial
vegetables provide food and medicine for people. The result is a front
yard that functions as a productive ecosystem instead of a decorative
lawn. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}







What You'll Learn From This Tour




How a front yard can become an edible landscape without sacrificing
beauty or biodiversity.



Why regional native plants provide essential habitat for birds,
pollinators, and beneficial insects while growing alongside food crops.



How a living fence creates privacy, wildlife habitat, and year-round
ecological value instead of relying on conventional hedges.



Why shade-tolerant native shrubs become increasingly valuable as a food
forest canopy matures.



How rainwater harvesting can support productive gardens while reducing
dependence on municipal water supplies.



Why community workshops and shared learning are central to Finca
Morada's mission of increasing resilience through gardening.









The Story Behind Finca Morada


Every garden has a history, and Finca Morada begins with honoring the
people and place that came before. Cris explains that the property was
already known throughout the neighborhood as the "purple house"
because the previous owner loved the color purple. Rather than erase
that history, the name Finca Morada—Spanish for "Purple
Farm"—preserves that connection while giving the property a new
purpose rooted in food, ecology, and community.



The half-acre property has evolved since 2019 into an educational urban
food forest containing more than 200 species of edible, medicinal,
native, and support plants. Instead of viewing the garden simply as a
collection of plants, the team describes it as a practice of
reconnecting with the land and rediscovering land-based ways of living,
even within a dense urban neighborhood. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}







A Living Fence Instead of a Conventional Hedge


One of the first things visitors notice is that the property doesn't
hide behind a row of identical shrubs. Instead, the front boundary is a
living fence composed of roughly thirty regional native species from
South Florida and the wider Caribbean. These plants demonstrate that a
privacy screen can also become wildlife habitat, educational space, and
an expression of local ecology.



Regional native plants from areas such as the Bahamas, Cuba, and the
Yucatán Peninsula are well adapted to South Florida's climate and help
support birds, butterflies, and pollinating insects. By combining
multiple native species rather than planting a single hedge, the garden
creates year-round diversity in structure, flowers, fruit, and habitat.



For neighbors walking past the property, the living fence quietly
demonstrates another possibility for urban landscapes—one that values
ecological diversity instead of uniformity.





Native Plants and Edible Plants Can Grow Together


One of the most valuable lessons from Finca Morada is that gardeners
don't have to choose between supporting wildlife and producing food.
Throughout the front yard, regional native plants grow alongside
bananas, papayas, edible groundcovers, medicinal herbs, and tropical
fruit trees. Rather than separating ornamental landscaping from food
production, every layer contributes to the health of the ecosystem.



Native plants attract birds, butterflies, and beneficial insects while
also providing shelter and nesting habitat. Many edible species benefit
from the increased biodiversity, and the wildlife in turn helps with
seed dispersal, pollination, and natural pest management. Instead of
competing with one another, native and edible plants become partners in
creating a healthier landscape.



This layered approach also creates a more resilient garden. Different
species occupy different ecological niches, reducing the dependence on
any single plant while increasing overall diversity and seasonal
interest.







Designing Every Layer of the Food Forest


As food forests mature, sunlight becomes increasingly limited beneath
the canopy. Finca Morada demonstrates why selecting plants for every
layer of the landscape is so important. Tall trees eventually provide
shade, but productive gardens continue beneath them through carefully
chosen understory shrubs, herbs, perennial vegetables, and native
groundcovers.



Many regional native shrubs naturally evolved beneath larger forest
trees, making them well suited for these shaded conditions. Species such
as beautyberry and wild coffee continue providing habitat and seasonal
interest while occupying spaces that many fruit trees cannot. At the
same time, edible plants like longevity spinach and Cuban oregano make
productive use of the lower layers of the garden.



Thinking vertically rather than horizontally allows the property to
produce more food, support more wildlife, and create a richer ecological
community without requiring additional space.







Plants Featured During the Tour


The front yard introduces visitors to an impressive diversity of native,
edible, and medicinal plants that work together throughout the
landscape. Some primarily provide food, while others attract wildlife,
improve soil, support pollinators, or offer traditional medicinal
uses. Together they illustrate how diverse planting creates healthier
and more resilient urban ecosystems.




Longevity Spinach — An edible perennial groundcover growing beneath larger plants.

Dwarf Namwa Banana — A compact banana variety producing full-sized fruit in a smaller space.

Papaya — Fast-growing tropical fruit tree integrated among native species.

Cuban Oregano — Aromatic medicinal herb commonly grown throughout tropical gardens.

Beautyberry — Native understory shrub known for vibrant purple berries and mosquito-repelling foliage.

Wild Coffee — Shade-tolerant native shrub that produces berries enjoyed by birds.

Cocoplum — Native fruiting shrub that functions as both edible landscape and living hedge.

Surinam Cherry — Productive edible hedge producing small tropical fruit.

Gumbo Limbo — Iconic South Florida native tree supporting tropical hardwood ecosystems.

Dade County Pine — Historic native pine once common throughout Miami-Dade County.

Sensitive Mimosa — Native groundcover recognized for leaves that fold when touched.

Porterweed — Pollinator favorite attracting butterflies throughout the growing season.

Bananas — Including larger Burro bananas connected to the rainwater harvesting overflow.








Community Education Through Gardening


Finca Morada is more than a productive garden. Nearly every major
project on the property becomes an opportunity to teach others. When
the team installed their 500-gallon rainwater harvesting system, they
invited community members to participate in a free workshop so everyone
could learn the process together.



That philosophy extends throughout the property. The goal is not simply
to create one successful homestead, but to help more people reconnect
with the land, increase neighborhood resilience, and develop practical
skills that can be replicated elsewhere. By openly sharing knowledge,
Finca Morada turns gardening into community education rather than a
private hobby.



This emphasis on education reflects one of the defining characteristics
of the property: every plant, every project, and every tour becomes an
opportunity to inspire others to imagine new possibilities for their own
yards.





Plant Collection Overview


Although this tour focuses primarily on the front yard, it introduces a
remarkable diversity of regional native plants, edible crops, medicinal
species, and support plants. Many of these species perform multiple
functions—feeding people, supporting wildlife, improving biodiversity,
or occupying different layers within the food forest.

Equally important is the philosophy behind the garden. Community

    tropical fruit grow together through careful pruning and desert
    microclimates.

      Cedar

Cedar’s Glendale property begins with a highly productive front yard
orchard built around peaches, apricots, figs, berries, and a growing
collection of experimental subtropical plants. Throughout the tour, he
shares which varieties have produced reliably, where pruning decisions
created problems, and how shade from vigorous trees helps less
heat-tolerant plants survive the Sonoran Desert.





  
    Garden
    Cedar’s Front Yard

Inside Cedar’s Glendale Front Yard Orchard


The front yard is centered around several low-chill peach varieties
selected for the Phoenix area. Tropic Snow, Florida Prince, and Desert
Gold each provide a different harvest window, flavor, and growth habit,
allowing Cedar’s family to pick peaches across more of the warm season.



The trees are highly productive, but that abundance creates its own
challenges. Heavy crops can pull branches downward or break limbs,
especially when trees are trained too wide. Cedar has begun moving away
from an extremely open goblet shape and is training new growth slightly
more upright to maintain stronger structure.



Apricots, mulberries, figs, blackberries, persimmons, and experimental
seedlings fill the spaces around the peaches. Together they create a
front yard that is both a working orchard and an ongoing test of which
fruit crops can perform reliably in Glendale’s heat.







What You’ll Learn From This Arizona Food Forest



  
    How Tropic Snow, Florida Prince, and Desert Gold peaches differ in
    flavor, vigor, harvest timing, and productivity
  

  
    Why heavily loaded peach trees need aggressive thinning and strong
    branch structure
  

  
    How vigorous mulberries can provide fruit and valuable afternoon
    shade for less heat-tolerant plants
  

  
    Why hot walls and reflected heat can create dangerous microclimates
    even when a planting area appears protected
  

  
    How cuttings and seedlings allow gardeners to test figs, white
    sapotes, peaches, cherimoyas, and other fruit at low cost
  

  
    Why Cedar evaluates each plant by productivity, fruit quality,
    climate tolerance, and the role it serves in the larger landscape
  








Growing Low-Chill Peaches in Glendale


Tropic Snow is a white-fleshed freestone peach that flowers early but
ripens later than Cedar’s other peach trees. The fruit is sweet with
relatively little tartness, and the tree can continue producing into
mid-July. Its broad growth habit has also shown Cedar why peach trees
need to be trained with future crop weight in mind.



Florida Prince is the family favorite for flavor, combining sweetness
with noticeable tartness. A warm winter caused the tree to flower and
ripen earlier than usual, and extensive winter pruning reduced the crop
but helped Cedar begin correcting a structure that had become too wide.



Desert Gold is the most vigorous and productive peach in the front yard.
Even after Cedar removed hundreds of young peaches, the remaining crop
still weighed branches downward. The tree handles summer heat well, but
its heavy production requires thinning, netting, and repeated pruning
to prevent broken limbs and keep fruit within reach.







Apricots, Mulberries, and a Developing Desert Canopy


Cedar’s Katy apricot has become more productive as it matures. The fruit
is mostly sweet and relatively small, but the tree now provides daily
harvests during its season. Cedar hopes to use some of the crop for jam,
where the mild fruit can gain additional flavor and usefulness.



Nearby, a Pakistan mulberry functions as both a fruit tree and a major
shade tree. Cedar cuts it back to roughly seven feet during winter, yet
it can add around fifteen feet of growth during the warm season. The
large canopy protects nearby plants from harsh western and northern
exposure while still producing fruit enjoyed by the family.



This relationship shows how a desert food forest can become easier to
grow as it matures. A vigorous support tree may eventually create the
cooler root zones and filtered afternoon light needed by persimmons,
mango seedlings, berries, and other sensitive plants.







Figs, Berries, and Experimental Fruit Trees


Several of the most promising plants began as small cuttings or
seedlings. A Peter’s Honey fig and Tiger Panache fig both started as
tiny cuttings shared by another grower. After only a few seasons, they
are carrying substantial crops, demonstrating how quickly figs can
become productive in Arizona when given a suitable location.



A Prim-Ark Freedom blackberry produces unusually large fruit but shows
clear stress from afternoon sun. Cedar is allowing a nearby Hong Kong
orchid tree to develop into a shade canopy that may eventually improve
the berry’s microclimate. The same section previously lost plants
because surrounding walls trapped heat and functioned like an oven.



White sapote, peach, starfruit, cherimoya, mango, and other seedlings
remain experiments. Some may eventually produce worthwhile fruit, while
others can become rootstock for proven varieties. Cedar’s approach
allows the garden to keep evolving without requiring every young plant
to have a guaranteed outcome.







Plants Growing in Cedar’s Front Yard


Cedar’s front yard combines proven low-chill stone fruit with berries,
figs, subtropical trees, seedlings, shade trees, and ornamentals. The
collection is smaller than the backyard food forest, but each plant is
carefully evaluated for productivity, fruit quality, heat tolerance,
and its ability to improve the surrounding microclimate.

The Green Yard Takeaway




Cedar’s front yard shows that productive desert orchards require more
than choosing low-chill varieties. Heavy crops must be thinned, branches
need to be trained for strength, and the heat reflected from walls can
be just as important as the amount of direct sunlight a plant receives.



The garden also demonstrates the long-term value of building living
shade. Vigorous trees such as mulberries can provide fruit while
creating the protected conditions needed by berries, persimmons,
seedlings, and subtropical experiments. Over time, the front yard
becomes more than an orchard—it becomes a network of increasingly
useful microclimates.

backyard contains an even larger collection of tropical fruit, grafting
experiments, grapes, figs, pomegranates, bananas, avocados, and other

In Part 2 of our visit to Food Forest Florida, Ryan guides us through
several productive growing systems designed for Central Florida. The
tour includes a young syntropic garden, a Grocery Row Garden, biomass
production, cold-tolerant avocados, low-chill fruit trees, container
fruit, rainwater collection, a pineapple island, and a diverse mango
orchard recovering from a winter freeze.

    Food Forest Florida

Inside Ryan’s Productive Agroforestry Systems


Ryan’s property contains several different growing systems, each
designed to test practical ways of producing food in Central Florida.
Some areas are planted with established named fruit varieties, while
others are filled with inexpensive seedlings, rooted cuttings, bananas,
nitrogen-fixing trees, and fast-growing biomass plants.



The systems are designed to do more than simply hold fruit trees.
Support plants create shade, protect sensitive crops from Florida’s
intense sun, reduce moisture loss, produce organic material, and help
build fertility directly within the landscape.



Instead of purchasing every input, Ryan is working toward a system
that produces its own mulch and green manure. Mexican sunflower,
vetiver, bananas, eucalyptus, nitrogen-fixing trees, and fast-growing
grasses are repeatedly cut and returned to the soil around productive
fruit trees.







What You’ll Learn From This Central Florida Food Forest



  
    How Ryan combines target fruit trees with fast-growing support
    species in a young syntropic garden
  

  
    How Mexican sunflower, vetiver, bananas, and grasses can produce
    chop-and-drop fertilizer
  

  
    How a three-row Grocery Row Garden fits fruit trees and biomass
    production into a compact space
  

  
    How seasonal avocado varieties may extend the Florida avocado
    harvest across much of the year
  

  
    Why Ryan keeps certain mangoes, apples, and avocados growing in
    containers
  

  
    How seven rain barrels store approximately 400 gallons of water
    for the garden
  








Four Highlights From the Food Forest Florida Tour



  

    

      
      

    

    

      Grow Your Own Fertilizer With Chop and Drop

      
        Ryan uses fast-growing support plants to create mulch, green
        manure, shade, and nutrients directly inside the food forest.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      A Pear Soaked in Brown Sugar?

      
        Silas Woods sapodilla remained productive through the freeze
        and produces sweet fruit with a rich brown-sugar flavor.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      Ryan’s Grocery Row Garden System

      
        Two productive tree rows surround a central biomass row that
        continually produces organic material for the fruit trees.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      Growing Fruit Trees in Containers

      
        Container-grown mangoes, apples, and avocados can remain
        productive while still being moved when freezing weather arrives.
      

    

  







Building Fertility With Syntropic Agroforestry


Ryan's newest planting area is inspired by syntropic agriculture, a
style of agroforestry that focuses on producing fertility directly
inside the garden. Rather than relying primarily on purchased compost
or fertilizer, the system grows fast-growing support species whose
biomass is continually recycled back into the soil.



Nitrogen-fixing trees such as Enterolobium establish the future
canopy, while Mexican sunflower, vetiver grass, bananas, and other
rapid-growing plants provide a continual supply of organic material.
These plants are repeatedly cut and returned to the soil through
chop-and-drop, helping retain moisture, feed soil biology, reduce
weed pressure, and gradually improve fertility.



Ryan also incorporates perennial vegetables and understory species
beneath the developing canopy so the garden begins producing food long
before the larger trees reach maturity. The result is a system where
every layer serves multiple purposes—from food production to shade,
mulch, pollinator support, and nutrient cycling.







The Grocery Row Garden System


One of Ryan's signature projects is the Grocery Row Garden, adapted
from David the Good's design. The concept is simple: two rows of
productive fruit trees surround a center row dedicated almost entirely
to biomass production.



Rather than planting another row of fruit trees, the middle bed grows
species whose primary purpose is producing organic matter. Fast-growing
grasses and chop-and-drop plants are harvested multiple times each
year and spread beneath the surrounding fruit trees as green manure.
This continually feeds the system while reducing dependence on outside
inputs.



Ryan begins new Grocery Row plantings by loosening compacted soil a
single time, adding compost to quickly reintroduce soil biology, and
covering everything with deep wood chips. Once established, biomass
plants become the primary source of fertility for the surrounding
orchard.







Growing Fruit Trees for Long Harvest Seasons


Another theme throughout the property is extending harvest windows.
Instead of planting only one avocado or loquat variety, Ryan selects
multiple cultivars that ripen at different times. Winter Mexican,
Mexicola Grande, and Brogdon avocados together can provide fruit over
much of the year, while carefully selected loquat cultivars extend the
spring harvest beyond a single short season.



Many additional trees are grown from seed as long-term experiments.
Some will eventually be grafted with improved varieties, while others
may prove to be worthwhile selections on their own. Seedlings also
provide inexpensive rootstock for future propagation.



This willingness to experiment allows the property to function as both
a productive food forest and an ongoing learning laboratory.







Container Fruit Trees and Freeze Protection


Not every fruit tree grows in the ground. Ryan intentionally keeps
certain mangoes, apples, and avocados in large containers so they can
be moved during freezing weather.



Low-chill apple varieties such as Anna and Dorsett Golden continue to
produce successfully in pots, while compact mango cultivars including
Honey Kiss and Pickering remain portable enough to protect when
necessary. Even Wurtz avocado can remain productive in containers for
many years with proper care.



Container growing gives gardeners an opportunity to expand the number
of species they can grow while reducing the risk associated with
occasional Florida freezes.







Plants Growing in Ryan's Agroforestry Systems

experiments, nitrogen-fixing support trees, perennial vegetables,
biomass crops, tropical fruit, and low-chill temperate species working

The Green Yard Takeaway




Ryan’s property shows that productive agroforestry is not only about
growing more fruit trees. The larger goal is to design a system where
shade, mulch, fertility, water, protection, propagation, and food
production reinforce one another.



The most important lesson is Ryan’s effort to grow many of his own
inputs. Fast-growing grasses, nitrogen-fixing trees, bananas, Mexican
sunflower, vetiver, and other support plants produce material that can
be cut and returned directly to the soil. Over time, this can reduce
dependence on purchased fertilizer while improving moisture retention
and soil health.



The property also demonstrates the value of diversity. Cold-tolerant
avocados, low-chill temperate fruit, tropical species, container-grown
trees, seedlings, grafted cultivars, rainwater storage, and multiple
planting systems create several different paths to productivity within
the same Central Florida landscape.

    tropical fruit trees, perennial vegetables, pollinator plants, and rare

      Host
      KC at Gonza Gardens
    

    
      Published
      July 10, 2026
    

  





In Part 2 of our visit to Gonza Gardens, KC takes us through the
backyard, side yard, raised beds, nursery propagation area, and an
astonishing collection of tropical and subtropical plants growing in
Tampa, Florida. This densely planted residential food forest combines
fruit production, perennial vegetables, rare ornamentals, wildlife
habitat, and plant propagation within the same landscape.

    Gonza Gardens

    KC

    Tropical Fruit Diversity
  






Inside a High-Density Tampa Food Forest


KC and her family originally began developing the backyard as a garden
filled with rare ornamentals collected from around Florida. As their
interest in food forestry grew, edible plants were layered into the
existing landscape, creating a garden where beauty, food production,
and wildlife habitat all overlap.



The result is not a conventional orchard with widely spaced trees.
Mangoes, sapodillas, mulberries, avocados, white sapotes, jackfruit
relatives, perennial vegetables, flowering plants, vines, ponds, and
nursery stock are fitted into nearly every available part of the
property.



Many trees are pruned to remain reachable, while grafting allows
several proven varieties to grow on a single tree. Upper-canopy plants
also provide shade and protection for sensitive tropical species,
helping KC grow plants that might otherwise struggle during Tampa’s
occasional cold weather.







What You’ll Learn From This Tampa Food Forest



  
    How KC layers fruit trees, shrubs, vines, ornamentals, and
    perennial vegetables into a residential property
  

  
    Why grafted trees can provide more predictable fruit than
    unknown seedlings
  

  
    How pruning keeps mulberries and avocados productive and
    easier to harvest
  

  
    How ponds and fountains support birds, frogs, lizards,
    pollinators, and other wildlife
  

  
    Why Florida gardeners often need tropical alternatives to
    lettuce, apples, peaches, pears, and other temperate crops
  

  
    How canopy cover and warmth from the house help protect
    sensitive plants such as coffee and cacao
  








Five Highlights From the Gonza Gardens Tour



  

    

      
      

    

    

      This Tropical Fruit Replaces Apples in Tampa

      
        KC explains why jujube can be a productive alternative to
        apples in a climate with very few winter chill hours.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      Florida’s Most Underrated Fruit Tree?

      
        White sapote is cold tolerant, productive outside the main
        summer fruit season, and still unfamiliar to many growers.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      One of the Coolest Flowers in a Food Forest

      
        Dutchman’s pipe produces unusual flowers and serves as a host
        plant for the Polydamas swallowtail butterfly.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      Grow a Pineapple Patch From Store-Bought Tops

      
        Store-bought pineapple tops can be rooted and replanted,
        eventually becoming an expanding patch of homegrown pineapples.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      This One Tree Grows Three Different Mulberries

      
        KC shows how Shangri-La, Chiang Mai 60, and Skinner mulberries
        can grow together on a single grafted tree.
      

    

  








Growing Tropical Fruit in Tampa, Florida


One of the strongest lessons from Gonza Gardens is the importance of
choosing plants that want to grow in the local climate. KC explains
that many of the apples, peaches, plums, pears, lettuces, peppers, and
large tomatoes they initially tried were poorly suited to Tampa’s heat
and limited winter chill.



Instead of repeatedly struggling with those crops, the garden now
relies more heavily on subtropical and tropical alternatives. Jujube
fills a role similar to a small apple, while moringa, katuk, longevity
spinach, Okinawa spinach, and edible hibiscus provide perennial leafy
greens better adapted to Florida’s heat.



White sapote is especially useful because it tolerates cooler weather
and may provide fruit outside the main mango-heavy summer season. This
helps spread harvests across more of the year rather than having every
major fruit crop ripen during the same few months.







Food Forest Design: Pruning, Grafting, and Dense Planting


KC keeps several trees intentionally small. Mulberries are repeatedly
pruned because fruit growing beyond reach often becomes bird food,
while everbearing varieties such as Chiang Mai 60 can flower and
produce again following pruning.



Grafting allows the garden to hold more varieties without requiring a
separate mature tree for every cultivar. One mulberry carries three
varieties, while sugar apple, white sapote, and other trees are being
top-worked or grafted to improve fruit quality, pollination, and
overall reliability.



Because the property is densely planted, KC considers the future growth
habit and vigor of each tree. Slow-growing star apples can be planted
relatively close and trained in opposite directions, while faster
canopy trees such as ice cream bean and Cecropia occupy the upper layer.







Creating Wildlife Habitat in a Food Forest


The garden is designed to feed more than people. Firebush, porterweed,
firespike, powderpuff, cassia, Dutchman’s pipe, dill, citrus, and other
plants attract or support hummingbirds, butterflies, caterpillars, and
pollinating insects.



KC also intentionally provides water through ponds and fountains. She
has observed that birds may damage less fruit when clean drinking water
is readily available. The same water features support frogs, lizards,
neighborhood cats, and the larger backyard ecosystem.



Rather than treating insects and wildlife as separate from the garden,
Gonza Gardens includes their interactions as part of a functioning
food forest.

    by-appointment tropical plant nursery and productive fruit farm

      Host

      Bee at Beez Tropical Garden

    

    

      Published

      January 26, 2026

    

  






At Beez Tropical Garden, visitors do not have to imagine what the small
trees offered by a nursery might eventually become. Young plants share
the property with productive tropical fruit trees that have been
growing in Homestead for twenty to thirty years, creating a living
reference collection where gardeners can observe mature size, growth
habit, shade patterns, flowering, and fruit production. As Bee guides
us through the nursery and orchard, every pathway reveals another
unfamiliar fruit, useful herb, medicinal species, or edible plant with
a story connected to culture, food, and tropical horticulture.

    Beez Tropical Garden

Inside Beez Tropical Garden


Beez Tropical Garden combines a working tropical fruit farm, mature
orchard, and by-appointment nursery on the same Homestead property.
Young plants grow near established trees, allowing visitors to see what
a small nursery purchase may eventually become after decades in South
Florida.



The collection extends far beyond familiar mangoes and avocados.
Tropical fruit trees share the landscape with medicinal plants,
culinary herbs, perennial vegetables, fragrant foliage, vines, and
shade-tolerant understory species.



As Bee introduces each plant, the tour becomes an outdoor lesson in
fruit quality, mature tree size, traditional uses, local growing
conditions, and the value of preserving unusual tropical species.







What You’ll Learn From This Tropical Nursery Tour



  
    How a tropical nursery and productive fruit farm can operate
    together on one property
  

  
    Why seeing mature orchard trees helps gardeners make better
    planting decisions
  

  
    How tropical fruit, culinary herbs, medicinal plants, and perennial
    vegetables can share the same landscape
  

  
    Why mature size, shade, pruning needs, and harvest height matter
    before purchasing a young tree
  

  
    How specialty nurseries preserve rare plants and practical local
    growing knowledge
  

  
    Why edible landscapes can provide flavor, fragrance, culture, and
    education in addition to fruit
  








Two Highlights From Beez Tropical Garden



  

    

      
      

    

    

      A Mature Starfruit Tree on a South Florida Fruit Farm

      
        Bee shows a mature starfruit tree and explains how its fruit,
        flowers, and pollinator activity fit into the working orchard.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      This Tropical Fruit Tastes Like a Pear Dipped in Brown Sugar

      
        Bee introduces Alano sapodilla and describes its sweet,
        brown-sugar flavor while discussing the farm’s sapodilla
        collection.
      

    

  








Why Seeing Mature Tropical Fruit Trees Matters


A young nursery tree rarely reveals its future canopy, pruning needs,
harvest height, or effect on the plants around it. At Beez Tropical
Garden, visitors can walk beneath mature specimens and understand how
each species changes as it ages.



Established trees also show how an orchard evolves. Expanding canopies
create shade, alter airflow, drop organic matter, and open new
opportunities for herbs and perennial crops beneath them.



This helps gardeners ask better questions before planting: How large
will the tree become? Can it be kept within reach? What can grow below
it? Those questions often matter more than simply choosing a favorite
fruit.







Beyond Fruit: Herbs, Medicinal Plants, and Traditional Uses


Although fruit trees form the upper canopy, the property also includes
aromatic herbs, medicinal plants, perennial vegetables, and useful
foliage crops. These species expand the garden beyond seasonal fruit
production.



Plants such as Cuban oregano, pandan, and the Root Beer Plant make the
tour memorable because they invite visitors to smell, taste, and
connect plants with culinary or cultural traditions.



Together, these lower layers demonstrate that abundance can include
edible leaves, fragrance, medicine, propagation material, and cultural
knowledge—not only baskets of fruit.







The Value of Specialty Tropical Nurseries


Large garden centers tend to focus on plants that are easy to produce
and sell at scale. Specialty nurseries preserve unusual fruit trees,
culturally important herbs, and lesser-known edible plants that may be
difficult to find elsewhere.



Beez Tropical Garden adds another layer by allowing visitors to see
young nursery stock beside mature examples. That combination of plants,
local experience, and long-term evidence makes the nursery especially
valuable to South Florida growers.



Every propagated cutting or young tree also helps move rare plants into
new gardens, keeping both the species and the knowledge attached to them
alive within the wider community.

The tour includes mature fruit trees, nursery stock, medicinal herbs,
culinary plants, perennial vegetables, aromatic species, and edible
ornamentals from tropical regions around the world.

  New Roots Community Farm






  Inside One of America’s Most Diverse Community Gardens

  

    California

    San Diego

    City Heights

    Community Gardens

    Urban Farming

    Cultural Gardening

    Food Access

    New Roots

  

  
    Tour New Roots Community Farm in San Diego, where 74 farmers from
    East Africa, Southeast Asia, Latin America, and other regions grow
    culturally important crops, share farming traditions, sell fresh
    produce, and build community through food.
  

  

    
      Guide
      Desiree at New Roots Community Farm
    

    
      Article Published
      August 6, 2026
    

  





New Roots Community Farm is more than a collection of garden plots. In
the middle of San Diego’s City Heights neighborhood, 74 farmers from
different parts of the world use the same land to grow food connected
to their families, cultures, health, and livelihoods. Walking through
the farm can feel like moving between countries as growing styles,
crops, recipes, and agricultural traditions change from one plot to the
next.





  
    Garden
    New Roots Community Farm
  

  
    Guide
    Desiree
  

  
    Location
    City Heights, San Diego
  

  
    Established
    2007

    74 Community Growers
