    Food, Culture & Community
  

  
    Tour Length
    Approximately 21 Minutes
  






Inside New Roots Community Farm


New Roots Community Farm was established in 2007 when a group of local
residents came together to create a place where people could grow their
own food. Some of the original farmers were still cultivating plots at
the time of the tour, giving the farm a sense of continuity that spans
many growing seasons.



The farm includes 74 growers from a wide range of backgrounds. Desiree
describes East African, South American, Central American, Cambodian,
Burmese, and other Asian farmers working throughout the property. Each
plot reflects the preferences, techniques, and foods important to the
people caring for it.



That diversity is visible in both the crops and the way they are grown.
Some farmers cultivate large stands of kale and collards, while others
harvest vegetables at a younger stage for microfarming. Some plots are
built around perennial crops, fruit trees, sugar cane, and bananas,
while others focus on herbs, greens, eggplants, beets, radishes, and
produce sold directly to local communities.







What You’ll Learn From This San Diego Community Garden



  
    How 74 farmers from different cultural backgrounds share one urban
    growing space in City Heights
  

  
    Why culturally familiar crops can support nutrition, identity, and
    a stronger connection to home
  

  
    How Cambodian, East African, Burmese, and Latino growers use
    different harvesting and planting methods
  

  
    How the community greenhouse supports seedlings, farmer education,
    and donation-based plant sales
  

  
    How hot composting and in-ground worm systems can process food waste
    for a working community farm
  

  
    How farmers sell produce through markets, restaurants, temples, and
    direct community relationships
  

  
    Why community gardens can improve food access while preserving
    agricultural knowledge across generations
  

  
    How shared land can create cooperation when individual farmers face
    theft, crop loss, or other setbacks
  








A Greenhouse Built by the Community


One of the first stops is the farm’s greenhouse, which farmers spent
more than 200 hours building. The structure gives growers a protected
place to start seedlings, propagate herbs, and prepare plants for the
coming season.



At the time of the visit, the greenhouse contained young plants being
prepared for spring. Some would eventually move into farmers’ plots,
while others were intended for a donation-based plant sale that could
help raise money for the farm.



The greenhouse also reflects an effort to make shared infrastructure
useful to more growers. Farmers start peppers, basil, mint, and seeds
connected to their own food traditions. Desiree hopes increased
participation will allow the space to become a stronger educational and
productive resource for the entire farm.







Chickens, Eggs, and Shared Farm Space


The farm also includes chickens managed by two community farmers.
Separate coops hold hens and roosters, producing eggs while adding
another layer of food production to the property.



The birds are regularly allowed to roam and exercise before being
guided back into their secure enclosures. Their presence demonstrates
how a community farm can include more than vegetable plots, even within
a dense urban neighborhood.



At the time of the tour, the farm was planning to move the coops toward
the back of the property. That change would open more of the front area
for events and other shared uses, showing how the physical layout
continues adapting to the community’s needs.







Growing Food Across Cultures


The strongest story at New Roots is the exchange of crops and knowledge
between farmers. East African growers cultivate large amounts of kale
and collards, harvesting individual leaves so each plant continues
producing rather than removing the entire crop at once.



Lemongrass illustrates how ideas move through the garden. Cambodian
farmers introduced the plant to East African growers, who came to value
its culinary and traditional uses. The exchange is a small example of
how people from different backgrounds influence one another simply by
growing beside each other.



Cambodian farmers often harvest mustard greens, amaranth, and other
vegetables at a smaller stage. Some sell produce at their temple on
weekends. Chayote vines are grown not only for the fruit but also for
the tender growing tips, which can be sautéed and eaten like a cross
between broccoli and spinach.



Burmese and Kenyan growers cultivate mint, amaranth, specialty
eggplants, Swiss chard, cilantro, and other foods familiar to their
families. The bitter flavor of certain small eggplants may be unusual
to some visitors, but it is exactly the quality those farmers want.







Composting Food Waste for the Farm


New Roots was rebuilding its composting area during the tour. The
system included three in-ground vermicomposting units along with three
above-ground hot composting systems.



The in-ground composters are designed to be relatively low maintenance:
food waste is added and worms carry out much of the decomposition.
Farmers maintain the hot composting systems more actively as part of
the shared work required to keep the farm productive.



The long-term goal was to process approximately 1,600 gallons of food
waste. The farm was also discussing a partnership with another San
Diego organization that produces organic waste through youth camps.
Redirecting that material to the farm could reduce disposal while
building soil for community growers.







Food for Families, Markets, Temples, and Restaurants


The produce grown at New Roots moves through several local food
networks. Some farmers grow mainly for their households, while others
sell at the City Heights Farmers Market, the Linda Vista market, local
temples, neighborhood restaurants, or directly to community members.



Kale and collards are especially important crops. Farmers supply fresh,
chemical-free greens to residents who recognize both the growers and
the cultural value of the food. Produce that does not sell at one
market may be purchased back or donated to a local foodshed rather than
being wasted.



Other growers sell specifically to East African restaurants in and near
City Heights. These relationships help restaurants obtain familiar,
locally grown ingredients while creating income opportunities for the
farmers producing them.



The farm is also known for sugar cane. In one story, a customer drove
from San Francisco to obtain cane for a wedding, only to learn that the
original crop had been stolen. Other East African farmers combined
their own harvests so he could return home with more than enough. That
moment captures the cooperative spirit behind the garden.







Building a Productive Plot From the Ground Up


Every plot at New Roots develops differently. One Latino farmer had
moved into her space only months before the tour and transformed a
nearly empty area by installing raised beds, bringing in organic soil,
and incorporating compost supplied through the farm.



Her motivation was closely connected to her children’s health. She
believed that growing food organically helped reduce problems her son
experienced with some store-bought produce. Whether a farmer is
motivated by health, culture, income, or access to familiar food, each
plot becomes a personal response to a real family need.



That individuality is one reason community gardens matter. The land is
shared, but every grower can shape a plot around the crops, methods, and
goals that are most useful to them.







Crops Growing at New Roots Community Farm


The farm contains a mix of annual vegetables, perennial food crops,
fruit trees, herbs, culturally important plants, and crops grown for
local markets. Because each plot is managed independently, the
collection changes with the season and with the farmers currently using
the land.

The Green Yard Takeaway




New Roots Community Farm demonstrates that abundance is not measured
only by the amount of food produced on one piece of land. Here,
abundance is also found in the people: 74 growers sharing seeds,
farming methods, recipes, labor, and crops connected to different parts
of the world.



The garden shows how edible landscapes can preserve culture while
creating new relationships. Cambodian growers introduce lemongrass to
East African neighbors. Farmers combine sugar cane when someone loses a
crop. Fresh greens move from individual plots to families, markets,
restaurants, temples, and local food programs.



New Roots is a reminder that gardens do more than feed people. They
create places where knowledge can travel, newcomers can rebuild a sense
of home, and neighbors can discover abundance together.

      Published

In Part 1 of our visit to Gonza Gardens, KC guides us through a
front-yard tropical food forest in Tampa, Florida. The property
combines more than 100 fruit trees, perennial vegetables, fragrant
ornamentals, native host plants, pollinator habitat, and medicinal
plants within just 0.17 acre.





  
    Garden
    Gonza Gardens
  

  
    Host
    KC

    Tampa, Florida
  

  
    Climate
    USDA Zone 10A

    Approximately 4 Years

    More Than 100

    High-Density Tropical Growing
  






Inside a High-Density Front-Yard Food Forest


Gonza Gardens demonstrates how a relatively small residential
property can support an extraordinary amount of edible diversity. KC
and her husband grow more than 100 fruit trees on approximately 0.17
acre while still incorporating pathways, ornamental plants, wildlife
habitat, propagation areas, and places for the family to use the yard.



The front yard is not arranged like a conventional orchard. Trees are
selected and positioned according to their mature size, vigor, growth
habit, cold tolerance, water requirements, and role within the canopy.
Some plants are trained upward, others are kept columnar, and vines are
espaliered along fences to use vertical space.



The garden originally began as an ornamental landscape before much of
it was converted into a food forest. That history remains visible in
the fragrant flowers and colorful foliage growing among mangoes,
avocados, mulberries, sapodillas, perennial vegetables, herbs, and
native butterfly host plants.







What You’ll Learn From This Tampa Food Forest



  
    How more than 100 fruit trees can be fitted into approximately
    0.17 acre through careful plant selection and pruning
  

  
    How KC protects sensitive tropical trees from cold by using the
    house, canopy layers, greenhouse covers, and planting orientation
  

  
    Why tropical alternatives such as Barbados cherry, jujube, and
    Vietnamese pomegranate can replace temperate fruits in Tampa
  

  
    How columnar pruning, espalier, grafting, and layered canopies
    increase diversity without requiring more land
  

  
    How roof runoff, French drains, mulch, and plant placement help
    support water-loving crops in Florida’s sandy soil
  

  
    How native vines, flowering ornamentals, and host plants support
    butterflies, hummingbirds, bees, and other wildlife
  








Five Highlights From the Gonza Gardens Tour



  

    

      
      

    

    

      The Only Pomegranate That Grows in Tampa

      
        KC explains why Vietnamese Red pomegranate succeeds where
        traditional varieties struggle with Tampa’s limited chill hours.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      The Secret to Protecting a Tropical Food Forest? Design!

      
        Thoughtful placement, canopy protection, and the warmth of the
        house help sensitive tropical plants survive damaging cold.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      This Mango Tree Held Fruit After a Historic Freeze?

      
        Orange Sherbet mango stood out after a historic freeze damaged
        many of the other mango trees growing throughout the property.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      You Can Grow PB&J in a Food Forest?

      
        Peanut butter fruit and blackberry jam fruit grow on opposite
        sides of the garden, creating a playful homegrown combination.
      

    

  


  

    

      
      

    

    

      100+ Fruit Trees in a High-Density Food Forest?

      
        KC and her husband use pruning, layering, and careful spacing
        to grow more than 100 fruit trees on only 0.17 acre.
      

    

  








Protecting Tropical Fruit From Cold in Tampa


The tour took place after a damaging winter freeze affected many of
the tropical trees. Mangoes and jackfruit showed substantial damage,
while the Orange Sherbet mango remained especially resilient. More
sensitive plants, including soursop, received temporary greenhouse
covers and thermostatically controlled heat.



Protection begins with the original food forest design. Sensitive
trees are placed on the south side of the house and maintained near
the height of the building, allowing cold north winds to travel over
them. Larger plants and upper-canopy trees also help shelter cacao,
coffee, breadfruit, Cecropia, and other tropical species growing below.



Not every tree can be enclosed or heated in a densely planted garden.
The larger strategy is therefore to combine thoughtful placement,
canopy layers, pruning, and selective protection so the landscape
works as a connected system.







Growing Tropical Alternatives in Florida


Many familiar temperate fruits and vegetables are difficult to grow
consistently in Tampa. Traditional cherries, apricots, apples,
pomegranates, lettuce, tomatoes, and cucumbers may struggle with heat,
humidity, disease, pests, or insufficient winter chill.



Gonza Gardens instead includes tropical and subtropical plants that
fill similar roles. Barbados cherry provides a cherry-like fruit rich
in vitamin C. Jujube can serve as an apple alternative. Vietnamese Red
pomegranate fruits despite limited chill, while tindora produces small
cucumber-like fruit and edible leaves through much of the year.



Perennial greens such as katuk, longevity spinach, and Okinawa spinach
also reduce the need to repeatedly grow heat-sensitive lettuce. The
garden’s productivity comes partly from choosing crops adapted to the
climate rather than continually forcing unsuitable plants to survive.







Food Forest Design for a Small Residential Property


High-density growing requires more than planting trees close together.
KC considers the vigor and mature growth habit of each cultivar before
choosing its position. Florigon mango is allowed to occupy more of the
upper canopy, while compact cultivars such as Honey Kiss remain smaller
and easier to prune.



Avocados are maintained in a narrow, columnar shape at approximately
ten feet tall. Blackberries are trained horizontally along the fence,
while sugarcane forms a productive living screen. Mulberries are
pruned frequently, which can stimulate repeated flowering on
everbearing varieties and keep fruit within reach.



Water requirements also influence placement. Bananas failed in a dry
front-yard location despite thick mulch, but Namwa banana became
productive when planted where roof runoff travels through a French
drain. That single plant can receive supplemental water from the
existing landscape instead of depending entirely on irrigation.







Creating Pollinator and Wildlife Habitat


Edible plants share the garden with native host plants, fragrant
flowers, and ornamentals selected for wildlife. Corky-stem passion
vine supports Gulf fritillary and zebra longwing butterflies, while
Dutchman’s pipe supports Polydamas and pipevine swallowtails.



Amistad salvia, native red salvia, porterweed, blue sky vine,
bougainvillea, Senna alata, sweet almond, and other flowering plants
provide nectar, fragrance, color, and extended bloom periods. Coontie
also serves as a host plant for the atala butterfly.



The result is a food forest that produces for people while also
providing habitat for butterflies, caterpillars, hummingbirds, bees,
and other wildlife throughout the property.







Plants Growing in the Gonza Gardens Front Yard


This portion of Gonza Gardens includes tropical fruit trees, named
cultivars, perennial vegetables, medicinal plants, spices, native
species, butterfly host plants, flowering ornamentals, and support

The Green Yard Takeaway




Gonza Gardens shows that the number of acres available matters less

The front yard also demonstrates the value of adapting to the local

Tampa, while roof runoff, canopy protection, native host plants, and
perennial vegetables allow the landscape to become more productive and
resilient over time.

Dense planting can create a food-forest environment rather than a conventional orchard layout.
Plant selection and placement matter when many species share a small area.
A residential landscape can become both productive and highly diverse.
